Lesson 1: The aircraft is only one part of the system

Course: Introduction to Drone Technology

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Estimated study time: 20-30 minutes including the desk exercise (author estimate).

Learning focus

Identify the aircraft, control station, command link and payload.

Lesson

A client asks for a map of a small construction site. Before choosing a drone, write down the result the client needs: a dated visual record, a measurable surface, or an inspection finding. These are different products. A sharp photograph does not automatically provide reliable measurements, and a model that looks complete can still contain gaps.

Think in four connected parts. The aircraft carries the equipment. The remote pilot station allows the crew to monitor and direct it. The command link carries instructions and status. The payload collects the useful information. The people, procedures and operating environment determine whether these parts can work together safely. A camera specification alone cannot describe mission capability.

A multirotor can hold position and inspect a small area from different directions, but carrying more mass affects its performance. A fixed-wing aircraft generally suits sustained forward travel; its launch, recovery and turning needs must fit the site. A hybrid combines operating modes with additional system complexity. These are selection considerations, not promises about a particular model.

Separate three questions in every equipment comparison: Can it collect the required information? Can the crew operate it within the relevant limitations and permissions? Can the team check and deliver usable results? Automation can help execute a planned path. It cannot establish that the path is safe, lawful, or suitable for the data product.

For the construction request, produce a short equipment decision with assumptions. If the client has not defined accuracy, inspection criteria, or output format, record those as questions rather than selecting the most expensive aircraft.

Desk exercise

Create a four-part system diagram for a fictional construction survey. Add one failure consequence and one verification step for each part.

Marking guide

A strong answer links aircraft, control station, command link and payload to the client deliverable. It distinguishes capture capability from permission and validation, and identifies missing client requirements.

DRAFT — STAFF REVIEW ONLY. Incomplete and unreviewed; not approved aviation training.

Lesson 1: Understand the motion before using the controls

Course: Drone Flight Fundamentals

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Estimated study time: 20-30 minutes including the desk exercise (author estimate).

Learning focus

Describe aircraft axes and basic motion.

Lesson

Use a simulator for this lesson. Keep propellers removed from any aircraft used only for desk familiarisation. The purpose is to connect control input, aircraft attitude and movement, not to teach an unsupervised first flight.

An aircraft has longitudinal, lateral and vertical axes. Roll, pitch and yaw describe rotation about those axes. Position describes where the aircraft is; attitude describes its orientation. They are related but different. A multirotor can change its attitude before a clear positional change becomes visible, so a pilot who reacts only to displacement may respond late.

In a simplified stationary hover, the upward component of thrust balances weight. Tilting the thrust vector introduces a horizontal component. If total thrust does not increase, its vertical component becomes smaller. This explains why a demand for horizontal acceleration also needs performance margin to maintain height. It does not provide a universal control setting: flight controllers and aircraft designs implement control differently.

Orientation changes the pilot's visual interpretation. A simulated aircraft facing the pilot makes a leftward aircraft motion appear on the opposite side of the pilot's viewpoint. Start by describing the aircraft's own orientation aloud. Avoid guessing from the screen location alone. A camera view and a map are useful aids, but they are not interchangeable with direct aircraft attitude awareness.

Before a simulator exercise, agree a starting state, exercise boundary, instructor intervention signal and stop condition. Afterwards compare intended movement with actual movement. Record one observation, its possible cause and the next controlled practice step. Better practice reduces uncertainty instead of rewarding a lucky recovery.

Desk exercise

In a simulator, annotate three screenshots showing roll, pitch and yaw. Explain one difference between aircraft-relative and pilot-relative directions.

Marking guide

Award credit for correct axes, separation of attitude and position, and a defined stop condition. Do not assess physical flight competence from screenshots.

Lesson 1: Start with the story and the delivery

Course: Aerial Photography and Videography

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Estimated study time: 20-30 minutes including the desk exercise (author estimate).

Learning focus

Translate a client brief into a shot list.

Lesson

A property client requests a short video showing the entrance, the relationship between buildings and the surrounding landscape. The useful first deliverable is a shot list. Each shot should answer a viewer question. An entrance overview establishes access; a wider view establishes location; a detail provides texture. Repeating the same view at several heights does not necessarily add information.

Specify the intended format before capture: orientation, duration, resolution, frame rate and delivery channel. These choices affect framing and editing. Keep a record of the client's priorities and any privacy restrictions. A request for an attractive result does not supply permission to film every neighbouring property or person.

Exposure decisions involve aperture where adjustable, shutter time and sensitivity. A longer exposure can introduce motion blur; a shorter one can make movement look more discrete. Increasing sensitivity may add visible noise. The appropriate compromise depends on the image and motion required. Avoid prescribing one setting for every aircraft, lens, light level and output.

Continuity is a planning problem. Adjacent shots should relate in direction, subject position and light. Prepare a sequence that can be edited without needing risky extra passes to repair missing coverage. Keep the original files, work from copies and record any transformations used in post-production.

For this lesson, plan with still images or a simulator. Evaluate whether every proposed shot advances the story and whether the finished edit can be delivered within the agreed scope. The grading criterion is deliberate communication, not the closeness of the aircraft to an obstacle.

Desk exercise

Produce a six-shot storyboard for a fictional property without flying. Include shot purpose, duration, framing, privacy consideration and delivery format.

Marking guide

Each shot should have a distinct purpose, a coherent sequence and a feasible delivery specification. Deduct for duplicated coverage presented as a complete story.

DRAFT — STAFF REVIEW ONLY. Incomplete and unreviewed; not approved aviation training.

Lesson 1: A map needs a measurement claim that can be checked

Course: Drone Mapping and Surveying

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Estimated study time: 20-30 minutes including the desk exercise (author estimate).

Learning focus

Distinguish a visual model from a validated measurement product.

Lesson

A project manager asks whether a stockpile has grown since last month. A visual model can show its shape, but a volume comparison requires a consistent boundary, reference surface, coordinate system and method. Begin with the decision the measurement will support and the tolerance needed. Do not select settings from the word mapping alone.

Ground sampling distance describes the approximate ground size represented by a pixel under stated geometry. It is not the same as positional accuracy. Blur, weak geometry, calibration, control quality, surface texture and processing choices can all affect the delivered result. A fine-looking raster does not establish survey-grade performance.

Control points help relate a model to a reference frame. Independent checkpoints are withheld from that adjustment and used to assess performance. If every surveyed point is used to fit the model, the residuals at those fitted points cannot serve as an independent test. Record point roles before processing and keep their measurement provenance.

Horizontal and vertical references must be stated. A height may refer to an ellipsoid or to a local height system; mixing them can create a systematic offset. Record coordinate units and the transformation used, including any required grid files or assumptions. On-screen alignment is insufficient evidence of a correct transformation.

For the stockpile scenario, define the same base surface and boundary rules for both dates, inspect coverage, and report uncertainty and exclusions alongside the change. A delivery note should let another analyst understand what was measured and what remains uncertain.

Desk exercise

Write a one-page quality plan for a fictional stockpile comparison, separating control and checkpoints and naming the information still required from the client.

Marking guide

Expect explicit units, reference frames, independent checks, comparable base surfaces and a stated acceptance tolerance. GSD alone must not be presented as accuracy.

Lesson 1: Sell a defined outcome with visible assumptions

Course: Commercial Drone Operations

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Estimated study time: 20-30 minutes including the desk exercise (author estimate).

Learning focus

Convert a client request into a scoped work order.

Lesson

A client asks for a roof inspection tomorrow and requests a fixed price immediately. A useful commercial response starts with scope. Ask what decision the inspection must support, which structures are included, what defects matter, and whether a qualified specialist must interpret the imagery. Capturing images and certifying a roof condition are different responsibilities.

Separate the work into preparation, capture, analysis and delivery. Preparation includes confirming access, operational feasibility, crew availability and required permissions. Capture depends on appropriate equipment and conditions. Analysis includes image review and traceable observations. Delivery includes agreed files, a reporting format and a review window. Omitting these stages from a quote does not remove their cost.

List assumptions that can change the work: access restrictions, weather, incomplete site information, additional structures, repeat attendance or a new reporting requirement. State who can authorise a scope change. A low initial price with an undefined deliverable creates disputes even when the flying is technically successful.

Define acceptance in terms the client can check. Examples include a complete agreed asset list, an image index, explicit limitations and the stated report format. Avoid promising that no defects exist merely because none were visible. Keep observed evidence separate from interpretation and from work outside the operator's competence.

Finish with a handover that explains naming, retention, permitted sharing and follow-up. Use fictional client information in the exercise. This course does not replace jurisdiction-specific operational approval, professional certification or a reviewed commercial contract.

Desk exercise

Draft a scope for a fictional three-building roof image survey, including exclusions, dependencies, acceptance criteria and a change request rule.

A complete response separates capture from specialist diagnosis, covers four work stages and includes clear acceptance criteria without unsupported safety claims.

DRAFT — STAFF REVIEW ONLY. Incomplete and unreviewed; not approved aviation training.

Lesson 1: Increase complexity one variable at a time

Course: Advanced Flight Techniques

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Estimated study time: 20-30 minutes including the desk exercise (author estimate).

Learning focus

Build a simulator progression from simple to complex tasks.

Lesson

Advanced performance is repeatable decision-making under a defined workload. It is not a collection of dramatic manoeuvres. Begin with a simulator baseline that the learner can complete consistently: stable orientation, a simple path and a deliberate stop. Document the conditions so the next exercise is comparable.

Increase only one demand at a time. A route can become more complex, a camera task can be introduced, or a simulated wind condition can change. Changing everything together prevents the instructor from identifying why performance deteriorated. A successful outcome after an uncontrolled recovery is not evidence of a reliable method.

Describe margins explicitly. Aircraft performance, attention, available space and time to respond are finite. A task that uses nearly all attention for framing may leave little capacity for monitoring warnings. More automation can change workload rather than simply reducing it. The crew still needs to understand what mode is active and what the aircraft will do when the plan changes.

For each exercise, define a normal completion criterion and an interruption criterion. The learner should be able to explain when to stop without treating that decision as failure. Record errors by observable behaviour: delayed recognition, incorrect mode assumption or an incomplete cross-check. Avoid vague judgements such as bad flying.

A progression plan should end with an instructor review of evidence, not a self-issued operational qualification. Real aircraft exercises require the appropriate training environment, instructor, permissions and aircraft-specific procedures. This opening lesson remains a desk and simulator activity.

Desk exercise

Design three simulator exercises that add one demand each. Include a stop condition and a measurable debrief question for every exercise.

Marking guide

DRAFT — STAFF REVIEW ONLY. Incomplete and unreviewed; not approved aviation training.

Lesson 1: Information is useful only within its place and time

Course: Weather and Airspace Management

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Estimated study time: 20-30 minutes including the desk exercise (author estimate).

Learning focus

Distinguish forecast, observation and site evidence.

Lesson

A weather forecast is a prediction for a place and period. An observation describes conditions at its reporting point and time. A site observation describes what the crew can currently see or measure nearby. These sources complement each other, but none automatically describes every part of the operating area.

Consider a site beside a ridge and large buildings. A regional wind forecast may not capture the local flow around those features. Note the source, issue time, valid period and location for each item. Then record where its applicability is uncertain. A gap in information should remain visible in the plan rather than being filled with a favourable assumption.

Airspace information also has boundaries and validity periods. A screenshot copied from a previous job can look authoritative while being unsuitable for today's place, time or activity. Establish a current information source, the applicable jurisdiction, the operating area and the relevant notices or restrictions. A map layer is a tool for interpretation, not permission by itself.

Combine the evidence with aircraft limitations and the operation's approved procedures. Define when the crew will reassess and what conditions require stopping. Avoid converting an illustrative classroom wind value or distance into a universal operating rule.

For the exercise, write a decision record rather than a weather prediction. Include the evidence used, the unresolved questions, who can resolve them, and the point at which the mission must be postponed. An explicit no-go can be the best supported professional outcome.

Desk exercise

Compare three fictional information records with different issue times and coverage. Decide which questions remain unresolved before a mission can proceed.

Lesson 1: Preserve the evidence before changing the system

Course: Drone Maintenance and Troubleshooting

Status: DRAFT. Original SkyScholar authoring; technical and instructional review pending.

Estimated study time: 20-30 minutes including the desk exercise (author estimate).

Learning focus

Separate a symptom from a diagnosis.

Lesson

A team reports intermittent vibration after replacing a propeller. The symptom is vibration under particular conditions. The recent replacement is relevant evidence, but it is not yet proof of the cause. Begin by recording the aircraft identification, configuration, part details, time of the change and when the symptom first appeared.

Follow the aircraft manufacturer's inspection and maintenance instructions. Do not improvise a live flight to reproduce an unexplained fault. A damaged or suspect propulsion component requires a safe stop and an appropriate technical review. Power down and isolate equipment according to its instructions before handling it. Battery damage, heat or swelling must be managed using the applicable manufacturer and site procedures.

Good troubleshooting changes one controlled variable at a time and states the expected observation. Record what was inspected, what was changed, who did it and what the result was. A software update, calibration or restart can alter the state and erase clues. Capture permitted diagnostic records first, without collecting unnecessary personal information.

Use a fault log with separate columns for symptom, evidence, hypothesis, test and result. A hypothesis can be rejected; that is useful progress. Replacing several parts together may restore operation but leave the cause unknown. Record that uncertainty honestly.

Return to service is a defined process with competent oversight, required checks and a record of release. This lesson teaches documentation and decision structure. It does not authorise repairs or override manufacturer limits.

Desk exercise

Complete a fictional fault log for vibration after a component change, identifying three useful records and two unsupported assumptions to avoid.

Marking guide

A good log preserves configuration, separates cause from timing, uses approved instructions and states who may release the aircraft back to service.

Learning focus

Lesson

A construction update can unintentionally capture workers, neighbouring homes or vehicle registrations. The fact that a sensor can record detail does not mean every detail belongs in the client's report or a public portfolio. Start by identifying who may be affected and why the information is needed.

Define the minimum useful data for the agreed purpose. Consider framing, timing, output resolution, access controls and retention. These are practical design choices. Relevant legal requirements and contractual permissions must be checked for the jurisdiction and project; an ethics checklist does not replace that review.

Truthful reporting is another part of professional conduct. State whether a finding is observed, inferred or unverified. Do not remove a limitation because a client prefers a more confident conclusion. A clear image can support a narrow observation while leaving the cause uncertain. If an error is discovered, retain a record of the correction and tell affected recipients which version supersedes the earlier one.

Respect the boundary of your competence. A pilot or image analyst should not imply a professional certification or specialist opinion that has not been provided. Attribute contributions and preserve permitted source provenance. Obtain explicit approval before using client material in marketing.

Status: DRAFT. Provisional South African subject; current syllabus mapping and competent review pending.

Objective

Lesson

Use a simplified multirotor model for this desk lesson. Weight acts downward. The aircraft's total thrust has a direction and magnitude. In a stationary level hover without other significant vertical effects, its upward component balances weight. This is an explanatory model, not a universal aircraft control setting.

When the aircraft tilts, the thrust vector tilts. Its vertical component becomes smaller if the total magnitude stays the same, while a horizontal component is introduced. Maintaining height while accelerating horizontally therefore requires an appropriate change in the total force balance. The flight controller's implementation depends on the aircraft.

Distinguish attitude, velocity and acceleration. Attitude is orientation; velocity describes motion; acceleration describes a change in velocity. A change in attitude need not produce the same immediate displacement in every environment. Wind and control response matter.

State assumptions before doing calculations. A diagram should name the aircraft type, axes, force directions and any effects omitted. Use the result to explain a concept, not to prescribe an unreviewed flight manoeuvre. Aircraft-specific performance and practical training belong in later reviewed lessons.

Navigation and flight planning: opening lesson

Status: DRAFT. Provisional South African subject; current syllabus mapping and competent review pending.

Objective

Keep time, distance and reference frames consistent.

Lesson

Navigation calculations are meaningful only when units and reference frames are consistent. In a simple constant-speed ground-track example, time equals distance divided by ground speed. Two kilometres is 2000 metres; at 5 metres per second, the calculated travel time is 400 seconds. That result excludes acceleration, turns, wind changes, reserve and every other omitted mission factor.

Heading describes the direction the aircraft is pointed. Ground track describes its movement over the ground. Wind can make these differ. A map line alone does not establish the heading, energy or clearance required to follow it.

Coordinate-reference systems give numerical coordinates geographic meaning. Degrees of latitude and longitude are angular units, not metres. Changing a layer's label is different from transforming its coordinate values. A display that aligns layers cannot by itself validate a measurement workflow.

In mapping work, independent checkpoints are held out from the fitting or adjustment process so they can provide an independent check. Keep their role separate from control points. A planning note should identify units, horizontal and vertical references, the information omitted and the checks needed before applying a calculation to a real operation.

Human factors: opening lesson

Status: DRAFT. Provisional South African subject; current syllabus mapping and competent review pending.

Objective

Make pressure and uncertainty visible in decisions.

Lesson

Human performance is part of the operating system. Workload, fatigue, attention and expectations affect how people interpret information and respond. A technically available aircraft does not establish that the crew is ready for the task.

External pressure can narrow attention. A client deadline, travel cost or desire to finish may encourage a person to dismiss contradictory evidence. Record the evidence and decision criteria before debating the commercial inconvenience of a delay. A stop decision supported by evidence can be a successful professional outcome.

Checklists support consistency, but reading words without checking the actual condition does not complete the purpose of a check. Clear role allocation and a shared understanding of intervention criteria help a team detect an omitted step or a mistaken assumption.

Use a debrief that separates observations from blame. Describe what happened, what information was available, what the team assumed and what process should change. Avoid inferring a person's medical condition or competence from a single error. The aim is a better decision system, with competent review where individual readiness is uncertain.

Status: DRAFT. Provisional South African subject; current syllabus mapping and competent review pending.

Objective

Resolve ambiguity before acting.

Lesson

Effective team communication makes the speaker, recipient, intended action and important conditions clear. In this desk lesson, use fictional crew roles and written messages. Operational radio phraseology, licensing and frequencies require current local references and competent instruction before practical use.

Ambiguity can arise from similar names, missing units, an unclear recipient or an unstated change of plan. A receiver should clarify uncertainty rather than choosing the most convenient interpretation. A response should demonstrate that the intended meaning was understood, not merely that a sound was heard.

Closed-loop communication includes a clear instruction or information item, an appropriate acknowledgement or readback, and confirmation or correction where needed. It is especially useful when a misunderstanding would have a material consequence. The exact required form depends on the approved procedure and context.

Keep operational records factual and proportionate. Record relevant changes and decisions without adding unnecessary personal information. After an unclear exchange, review the message structure and the team's process. Do not turn this general classroom model into a claim that a particular phrase is approved for live aviation radio use.
